meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In this sad world of ours, sorrow comes to all; and, to the young, it comes with bitterest agony, because it takes them unawares'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Lincoln: a private condolence letter of 23 December 1862 to Fanny McCullough. The signed one-page manuscript survives.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Lincoln’s letter to Fanny McCullough, written at the Executive Mansion in Washington on 23 December 1862, after her father Lt. Col. William McCullough was killed in Mississippi. The autograph letter signed survives, and the sentence appears in it word for word.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Autograph letter signed (“A. Lincoln”), 1 page, quarto — Shapell Manuscript Foundation
Roy P. Basler, ed., The Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln

source.excerpt:
Dear Fanny

It is with deep grief that I learn of the death of your kind and brave Father; and, especially, that it is affecting your young heart beyond what is common in such cases. In this sad world of ours, sorrow comes to all; and, to the young, it comes with bitterest agony, because it takes them unawares. The older have learned to ever expect it. I am anxious to afford some alleviation of your present distress. Perfect relief is not possible, except with time. You can not now realize that you will ever feel better. Is not this so? And yet it is a mistake. You are sure to be happy again.
trail: Lt. Col. William McCullough, Lincoln’s old friend from the Illinois circuit, was killed at Coffeeville, Mississippi, on 5 December 1862 ↗. At David Davis’s request, Lincoln wrote to his daughter Fanny on 23 December ↗.

The manuscript survives: Shapell describes an “Autograph Letter Signed (‘A. Lincoln’), as President, 1 page, quarto, Executive Mansion, Washington, D.C., December 23, 1862” ↗ and quotes the sentence from it.

The received text carries the line word for word — Abraham Lincoln Online prints the whole letter from Basler’s Collected Works ↗, and Dickinson College’s House Divided project gives the same text with scholarly commentary ↗.

Older printings differ. Project Gutenberg’s text of the Lapsley collected edition ↗ reads “In this sad world of ours sorrow comes to all, and to the young it comes with bittered agony because it takes them unawares” — a reminder that the punctuated version everyone quotes is the manuscript one.

author.name: Abraham Lincoln
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Abraham Lincoln led the United States through the Civil War and is remembered as much for his prose as his politics — the Gettysburg Address, the second inaugural, and a run of short private letters that do more emotional work in a paragraph than most writers manage in a chapter. He wrote this one by hand as a private condolence, not for publication. His own son Willie had died earlier that same year, which is part of why the letter lands: “I have had experience enough to know what I say.”

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with it
misattribution.intro: For once the famous name is the right one — this really is Lincoln, in his own hand. What gets mangled is the wording and the setting.

items.why: BrainyQuote runs it as one continuous sentence ending “…it takes them unawares. I have had experience enough to know what I say.” ↗ Those two sentences are not adjacent in the letter — four sentences sit between them — and the page gives no source at all.

Project Gutenberg’s text of the Lapsley collected edition ↗ prints “In this sad world of ours sorrow comes to all, and to the young it comes with bittered agony because it takes them unawares” — commas dropped, “bitterest” become “bittered” — and opens the letter with “deep regret” where the manuscript text reads “deep grief.”

It circulates as a free-floating aphorism about grief. It was a private note to a named young woman — Shapell, describing the manuscript, calls her “twenty-two year old Fanny McCullough” ↗ — and Lincoln wrote it only because David Davis asked him to ↗.

Lincoln’s other famous condolence letter is the contested one: scholars have debated whether his secretary John Hay wrote it, and the original has never been found ↗. The McCullough letter has neither problem.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Lincoln’s own, written 23 December 1862; the signed manuscript survives, and the standard text reads “…with bitterest agony, because it takes them unawares.” Read the whole letter ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: William McCullough was the kind of friend Lincoln made on the Illinois circuit: sheriff of McLean County for three terms, then clerk of the circuit court for four, missing an arm from a threshing accident and the sight of one eye from a gun that backfired at a parade ↗. He talked his way into the Fourth Illinois Cavalry anyway, and was killed at Coffeeville, Mississippi, on 5 December 1862 ↗.

His daughter Fanny took it badly enough to frighten people — she shut herself in her room and would neither eat nor sleep. David Davis, a friend to both families, asked Lincoln to write ↗, and he did, in the same grim December the Union army was wrecked at Fredericksburg. What he produced is one page, no rhetoric, no scripture — just a man telling a grieving young woman that she will be happy again, and that she should believe him because he knows.
detailsBody: The version everyone quotes is the manuscript version, which is unusual for a famous line. Basler’s Collected Works text — the one Abraham Lincoln Online prints ↗ — keeps Lincoln’s heavy, breath-marking commas and semicolon exactly as the popular quotation has them.

Earlier collected editions were tidier and less accurate. Project Gutenberg’s text of the Lapsley edition ↗ opens the letter with “deep regret” instead of “deep grief,” strips the punctuation out of the famous sentence, and garbles “bitterest” into “bittered.” If you have ever seen a comma-free version of this line, that family of printings is a plausible ancestor.
